meta.title: Remote Work Statistics 2026: Hybrid, Loneliness and Collaboration
meta.description: Sourced remote work statistics for 2026: how many people work from home, hybrid against remote, loneliness, collaboration, meetings and focus time, from BLS, Gallup, Microsoft and Buffer.

coverAlt: Mint and white bar-chart columns beside a small house with a mint roof, on a bright violet background.
title: Remote work statistics for 2026: who works remotely, and how it feels.
intro: In 2025, 35% of employed Americans did some or all of their work at home on the days they worked, and among US employees whose jobs can be done remotely, about eight in ten work remotely at least part of the week. Below are the numbers that matter for a team deciding how to work together: who works where, how lonely it is, how collaboration changes, and where the time goes. Every figure is from its original source, linked at the bottom, and checked on 3 November 2026. We make TinyFloor, a [virtual office](/virtual-office); the numbers aren't ours, and we've kept to what each source says.
takeaways: 35% of employed people in the US did some or all of their work at home on days they worked in 2025.
Of US employees with remote-capable jobs, 54% work hybrid, 25% fully remote and 21% on-site, as of August 2026.
25% of fully remote employees felt lonely a lot of the previous day, against 21% of hybrid and 16% of fully on-site employees.
When Microsoft moved to remote work, its 61,182 US employees' collaboration became more siloed, and communication moved from live to written.
68% of people say they don't have enough uninterrupted focus time in the workday.

sections.title: How many people work from home?
body: In 2025, 35% of employed people in the US did some or all of their work at home on the days they worked, and 70% did some or all of it at their workplace, according to the [Bureau of Labor Statistics' American Time Use Survey](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/atus.nr0.htm), released on 25 June 2026.

Who works from home varies a lot. Employed women were more likely to work at home than employed men, 38% against 31%. Among workers aged 25 and over, 51% of those with a bachelor's degree or higher did some work at home on days they worked, against 19% of those with a high school diploma and no college.

sections.title: How many employees are hybrid, remote or on-site?
body: [Gallup tracks US employees whose jobs can be done remotely](https://www.gallup.com/401384/indicator-hybrid-work.aspx). As of August 2026, 54% of them work hybrid, 25% work exclusively remote and 21% work on-site. Hybrid has held roughly steady since 2022.

What people would choose is different. Asked in November 2025, 61% of remote-capable employees preferred hybrid, 33% exclusively remote and 6% on-site. So fully remote work is less common than people would like (25% against 33%), and on-site work is far more common (21% against 6%).

items.title: Engagement by arrangement
items.body: Exclusively remote employees are the most likely to be engaged at work, 32%, then hybrid at 31% and on-site remote-capable employees at 28%.

items.title: Who sets the policy
items.body: Teams that set their hybrid policy together are the most likely to call it fair and say it helps collaboration, but as of May 2025 only 11% of employees work this way.

sections.title: Are remote workers lonelier?
body: On average, yes. In [Gallup's State of the Global Workplace 2024](https://www.gallup.com/workplace/645566/employees-worldwide-feel-lonely.aspx), 25% of fully remote employees said they had felt lonely a lot of the previous day, against 21% of hybrid employees and 16% of those who work only on-site. Across all employees worldwide the figure was one in five. Of everything Gallup analysed, work location showed the biggest difference in loneliness.

Remote workers say the same thing about themselves. In [Buffer's 2023 survey of 3,000 remote workers](https://buffer.com/state-of-remote-work/2023), the most common struggle, chosen by one in three, was staying home too often because there's no reason to leave, and the next was loneliness, at 23%. Yet 75% said they feel connected to their colleagues, mostly because they interact regularly or work well together.

sections.title: Does remote work change how teams collaborate?
body: The largest study is Microsoft's own. [Researchers used the emails, calendars, messages and calls of 61,182 US Microsoft employees](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41562-021-01196-4) in the first six months of 2020, when the whole company moved to remote work. Their collaboration network became more static and siloed, with fewer bridges between different parts of the company, and communication shifted from live to written. The authors suggest this may make it harder to pass new information across a company.

Remote workers notice it too. In [Buffer's survey](https://buffer.com/state-of-remote-work/2023), the things most often named as harder remotely were getting recognised by leadership (37%), collaborating (30%) and getting promoted (28%). And 62% said their immediate team spans several time zones, which leaves fewer hours to talk live at all.

sections.title: Where does the time go: meetings and focus?
body: In [Microsoft's Work Trend Index 2023](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/worklab/work-trend-index/will-ai-fix-work), 68% of people said they don't have enough uninterrupted focus time during the workday, and "inefficient meetings" was the top productivity disruptor they named.

Among [Buffer's remote workers](https://buffer.com/state-of-remote-work/2023), 75% spend between 1 and 10 hours a week in meetings: 52% spend one to five hours and 23% six to ten. Most like to be seen: 62% prefer to be on camera in video calls, mainly because it's easier to communicate when they can see someone's expression.

sections.title: What do these numbers mean for a remote team?
body: Our reading, not the sources': the numbers point at the same gap. Remote and hybrid work are here to stay, and people mostly like them, but fully remote people are lonelier and collaboration gets more siloed when the quick, unplanned conversations of an office go away. More meetings don't fill that gap, since people already say meetings eat their focus time.

What fills it is somewhere to be around each other without scheduling anything: seeing who's around, and talking for two minutes when it helps. That can be a habit, like a [virtual watercooler](/virtual-watercooler), or a place, like a [virtual office](/virtual-office) where you can [see who's in](/team-presence). For how teams already try it, see [Slack and Zoom, or a virtual office](/blog/slack-and-zoom-or-a-virtual-office), [a Discord voice channel for work](/blog/discord-voice-channel-for-work) and our guide to [building remote team culture](/guides/how-to-build-remote-team-culture).

faq.q: What percentage of people work from home in 2026?
faq.a: The latest US government figure is for 2025: 35% of employed people did some or all of their work at home on days they worked, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics' American Time Use Survey, released in June 2026.

faq.q: How many employees are hybrid or fully remote?
faq.a: Among US employees whose jobs can be done remotely, Gallup found in August 2026 that 54% work hybrid, 25% fully remote and 21% on-site. Asked in November 2025, 61% preferred hybrid, 33% fully remote and 6% on-site.

faq.q: Are remote workers lonelier than office workers?
faq.a: On average, yes. Gallup's State of the Global Workplace 2024 found 25% of fully remote employees felt lonely a lot of the previous day, against 21% of hybrid and 16% of fully on-site employees.

A study of 61,182 Microsoft employees, published in Nature Human Behaviour in 2021, found remote work made collaboration more siloed, with fewer bridges between groups, and moved communication from live to written.

faq.q: How much time do remote workers spend in meetings?
faq.a: In Buffer's 2023 survey of 3,000 remote workers, 75% spent 1 to 10 hours a week in meetings. Separately, 68% of people in Microsoft's Work Trend Index 2023 said they lack enough uninterrupted focus time.
